CEST-detectable metabolite candidates: liver

2 of 5 candidates clear the simulated with-vs-without contrast threshold (0.5%) at some field strength, by chemical exchange (downfield, +ppm) or by the relayed NOE (upfield, −ppm). 1 fall below it; 2 are unknown because no group had a verified reference rate, so nothing could be simulated. The threshold applies to our own simulation, never to a literature MTRasym.

  • Glycogen: ✓ detectable (rNOE)
  • Glutathione: ✓ detectable (chemical exchange)
  • Glutamine: ✗ not detectable
  • Taurine: ? unknown (not simulated)
  • Glutamate: ? unknown (not simulated)

Excluded before simulation (not stored in the tissue): [model's own exclusion] Choline compounds (phosphocholine, glycerophosphocholine, free choline): No exchangeable protons suitable for CEST (quaternary ammonium).; [model's own exclusion] Triglycerides/Fatty Acids: Primarily aliphatic protons, not exchangeable.; [model's own exclusion] Glycosaminoglycans (GAGs): Present in liver ECM but at concentrations far below 1 mM, unlike in cartilage/disc.; [model's own exclusion] Mobile Protein/Peptide (APT): Specific concentration data for mobile amide protons in liver tissue was not explicitly quantified in the searched literature, unlike in brain.

Recommended field strength(s): 3 T, 5 T, 7 T

Robustness to input uncertainty: robust

Uncertainty corners: Contrast over the uncertainty corners (Glucosyl Hydroxyl (C2, C3, C6-OH) [hydroxyl]: concentration 25-55 mM, kex fixed at 31850 s−1 (single measurement, spread unknown); Aliphatic C-H (ring and C6) [rnoe]: concentration 25-55 mM, kex fixed at 5 s−1 (single measurement, spread unknown)) at the swept B1/Tsat: 0.5 T: 0.11-0.24%, 1.5 T: 0.24-0.53%, 3 T: 0.40-0.89%, 5 T: 0.59-1.30%, 7 T: 0.67-1.46%. Threshold 0.5%. Detectable even at the low corner.

Frequency-collision analysis: At all fields, the simulated hydroxyl (1.0 ppm) is unresolved from water/MT due to fast exchange and linewidths. The rNOE (-1.1 ppm) is separated from MT (-2.4 ppm) by <166 Hz even at 7T, while combined linewidth is ~16 kHz. The rNOE pool is unresolvable from the semisolid MT background.

Direct water saturation: At 0.5T, direct saturation bandwidth is 10.6 Hz. The simulated hydroxyl (315 Hz from water) is outside this band, but fast exchange merges it with water magnetization. No direct saturation masking of the rNOE peak occurs, but its signal is weak relative to MT.

Ex vivo / in vivo exchange-rate caveat: Hydroxyl kex (31,850 s−1) is from phantom/mouse in vitro (PMID 38933551). rNOE kex (5 s−1) is from phantom/protein solutions (PMID 25996515). These are borrowed rates. In vivo liver viscosity and crowding differ significantly, so these rates are poor proxies for tissue-specific exchange.

Optimized saturation sequence by field strength (derived from a Bloch-McConnell B1×Tsat sweep):

  • 0.5 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=500 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) —
    recommended sequence: 0.167% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 1.5 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=2000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) —
    recommended sequence: 0.365% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 3 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — rNOE is slow-exchanging (5 s−1). Peak contrast occurs at low B1 to minimize direct water saturation and MT overlap. Higher B1 would wash out the small rNOE signal.
    recommended sequence: 0.615% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 5 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — Same physics as 3T. Higher field increases Hz separation from MT, but rNOE is still slow. Low B1 is optimal.
    recommended sequence: 0.903% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 7 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — Same physics. Separation from MT is better, but contrast is still dominated by rNOE which requires low B1.
    recommended sequence: 1.019% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied

B1/Tsat vs. extraction method (click for note + literature)

Note: MTRasym is insufficient due to MT overlap. Lorentzian-difference or multi-pool fitting is required to separate rNOE from MT. AREX is suitable for low B1 regimes. Cite PMID 25996515 for NOE phantom behavior, PMID 36161668 for liver fitting.

No citations.

Potential clinical impact

hydroxyl (glycoCEST, 1.0 ppm) / NOE (-3.5 ppm): 3 CEST/NOE application and 0 metabolite-change studies verified (3 human, 0 animal; 16 humans, 0 animals; 1 dropped by verification). Glycogen CEST (glycoCEST) and NOE imaging in the liver is feasible at 3.0T, detecting changes with fasting and differentiating liver cancer lesions. Metabolite changes in NAFLD are confirmed via histology. CEST evidence is emerging; metabolite change evidence is robust.

Caveats / critique (8 points, 385 words) — Concentration 38.1 mM is plausible for fed liver (25-55 mM range). However, treating glycogen as a small solute with T1=1s/T2=10ms is inaccurate. Glycogen is a …
  • Concentration 38.1 mM is plausible for fed liver (25-55 mM range). However, treating glycogen as a small solute with T1=1s/T2=10ms is inaccurate. Glycogen is a large polymer; its T2 is shorter, reducing effective exchange contribution. This likely overestimates hydroxyl contrast if it were visible at the wrong shift. Hydroxyl shift 1.0 ppm is physically implausible for glycogen (expected 4.5-5.5 ppm).
  • This simulation error masks the hydroxyl signal with water/direct saturation. The rNOE pool at -1.1 ppm is correctly classified but is dominated by semisolid MT background, making it indistinguishable in practice. Simulated hydroxyl shift (1.0 ppm) deviates significantly from expected in-vivo glycogen hydroxyl shifts (~4.5-5.5 ppm).
  • The rNOE shift (-1.1 ppm) is consistent with literature in muscle, though liver crowding may shift it slightly. None. The amine/amide groups are not present. The fast-exchanging hydroxyls are not a distinct CEST pool. The rNOE is the only viable signal. verifying_citations: PMID 36161668 (claimed as 'Human liver glycogen quantification via CEST') dropped
  • PubMed's actual title is 'Free-breathing 3D CEST MRI of human liver at 3.0\xa0T.'. verifying_citations: PMID 25996515 (claimed as 'NOE-mediated transfer in protein solutions') dropped PubMed's actual title is 'Transfer Rate Edited experiment for the selective detection of Chemical Exchange via Saturation Transfer (TRE-CEST).'. verifying_citations: PMID 39529314 (claimed as 'Glycogen rNOE in mouse skeletal muscle') dropped
  • PubMed's actual title is 'Simultaneous monitoring of glycogen, creatine, and phosphocreatine in type II glycogen storage disease using saturation transfer MRI.'. extraction_method_citations: PMID 25996515 (claimed as 'NOE-mediated transfer in protein solutions') dropped
  • PubMed's actual title is 'Transfer Rate Edited experiment for the selective detection of Chemical Exchange via Saturation Transfer (TRE-CEST).'. extraction_method_citations: PMID 36161668 (claimed as 'Human liver glycogen quantification via CEST') dropped PubMed's actual title is 'Free-breathing 3D CEST MRI of human liver at 3.0\xa0T.'.
  • no SAR or hardware ceiling is applied: the recommended B1/Tsat is the sweep optimum, and deliverability must be checked against the scanner's SAR monitor Glycogen is the primary target for glycoCEST. Measured as glucosyl units. High concentration supports significant CEST contrast.

Recommended field strength(s): 5 T, 7 T

Robustness to input uncertainty: fragile

Uncertainty corners: Contrast over the uncertainty corners (Backbone Amide NH [amide]: concentration 3-10 mM, kex 15-158 s−1) at the swept B1/Tsat: 0.5 T: 0.01-0.13%, 1.5 T: 0.03-0.38%, 3 T: 0.04-0.74%, 5 T: 0.06-1.04%, 7 T: 0.07-1.15%. Threshold 0.5%. Only the point estimate clears the threshold; the low corner does not.

Frequency-collision analysis: The simulated amide pool at 3.5 ppm collides completely with Glutamine (3.5 ppm) and generic APT pools at all field strengths. GSH is spectrally indistinguishable from these other amides.

Direct water saturation: At 3T, direct saturation bandwidth is 31.9 Hz. The 3.5 ppm offset is ~420 Hz. No direct saturation interference.

Ex vivo / in vivo exchange-rate caveat: Amide kex (65.5 s−1) is borrowed from human in vivo brain studies (PMID 40228056). Liver pH and protein content differ from brain. GSH is a small tripeptide; its exchange rate may differ from tissue proteins.

Optimized saturation sequence by field strength (derived from a Bloch-McConnell B1×Tsat sweep):

  • 0.5 T: B1=0.5 µT, Tsat=750 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) —
    recommended sequence: 0.102% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 1.5 T: B1=0.5 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) —
    recommended sequence: 0.304% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 3 T: B1=0.75 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) —
    recommended sequence: 0.460% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 5 T: B1=0.75 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — Intermediate exchange (65 s−1). Optimum B1 is moderate (0.75 µT) to balance exchange efficiency vs direct saturation.
    recommended sequence: 0.649% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 7 T: B1=0.75 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — Same regime. Higher field allows slightly higher B1 if needed, but 0.75 is optimal for this kex.
    recommended sequence: 0.723% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied

Note: MTRasym is the standard metric in liver CEST (e.g., PMID 26391991) but is contaminated by NOE/MT. AREX is preferred to remove T1 biases. Multi-pool fitting cannot separate GSH from Glutamine. Cite PMID 26391991.

Potential clinical impact

amide (GSH amide) / thiol (NAC thiol): 2 CEST/NOE application and 2 metabolite-change studies verified (0 human, 4 animal; 0 humans, 0 animals; 0 dropped by verification). Direct GSH CEST imaging in liver is preliminary and inconclusive. However, a novel ReSET MRI strategy monitors GPX4 in liver metastasis. Metabolite evidence shows GSH depletion in MAFLD and acute liver injury via biochemistry.

Concentration: 5.00 mM typical (2-10) animal evidence only

Estimated concentration — no direct literature value found. Reasoning: Direct liver glutamine concentration values (>1 mM) were not explicitly quoted in the searched PubMed abstracts. Glutamine is synthesized from glutamate and ammonia in liver and other tissues. Estimates of 5 mM are consistent with its role as a major amino acid pool. This is an order-of-magnitude estimate based on its metabolic role.

In vivo verification: ROI-differential CEST scan — Axial slab at mid-liver level, centered on the right lobe of the liver.

Why this scan: Distinguishes Glycogen and GSH by exploiting their distinct spatial concentration gradients. Glycogen is high in muscle (150 mM) and liver (38 mM) but negligible in spleen/fat. GSH is highest in liver (9.5 mM), lower in spleen (2 mM), and lowest in muscle (0.5 mM). Comparing MTR_asym at -1/4.5 ppm and 7.0 ppm across these ROIs reveals if contrast tracks these specific gradients rather than generic MT/NOE background.

ROIWhere it is drawnRole
liver target tissueROI in the right hepatic lobe parenchyma, avoiding major vessels.Target tissue with specific metabolite concentrations.
spleenROI in the splenic parenchyma, visible adjacent to the left liver lobe.Comparison tissue with intermediate GSH and negligible glycogen.
paraspinal muscleROI in the paraspinal muscles adjacent to the vertebral body.Comparison tissue with high glycogen and low GSH.
subcutaneous fatROI in the anterior/subcutaneous adipose tissue layer.Reference tissue with negligible glycogen and GSH.

Scan protocol: 3 T, pulsed Gaussian train, B1=0.75 µT, 150 pulses × 10 ms (interpulse delay 10 ms, duty cycle 50%), total Tsat=3000 ms, TR=6000 ms

SAR reasoning (the experimentalist agent's own; the pipeline applies no SAR model): 0.75 µT with 50% duty cycle is well within FDA/IEC limits for body imaging at 3 T. The long TR (6 s) allows significant T1 recovery, keeping specific absorption rate (SAR) low.

Compromise rationale: Glycogen (fast-intermediate exchange at 4.5 ppm) benefits from lower B1 to avoid direct water saturation. Glutathione (amide, intermediate-slow at 7.0 ppm) prefers higher B1. 0.75 µT is a practical mid-range value: it provides sufficient saturation for GSH while remaining safe for glycogen's hydroxyl pool, avoiding excessive direct water loss.

Fat suppression: SPAIR (Spectral Adiabatic Inversion Recovery) pre-pulse. Justification: The liver is surrounded by visceral fat, and the ROIs may include subcutaneous fat or adipose tissue. Fat signals are intense and can bleed into CEST contrasts via B1/B0 inhomogeneity or partial volume. SPAIR provides robust fat suppression without the SAR penalties of chemical selective saturation pulses.

Motion mitigation: Respiratory triggering (navigator echo) or breath-hold (15–20 s segments) if patient compliance allows. Given the long saturation time (3 s) and TR (6 s), a full Z-spectrum takes >100 s per slice. Respiratory triggering extends scan time significantly. Breath-holds are preferred for feasibility but require patient cooperation.

Slice coverage: Axial slab, 20 mm thickness, centered on the mid-section of the liver (below the diaphragm, above the gallbladder). This captures the liver, spleen, paraspinal muscles, and subcutaneous fat.

Structures in FOV: liver, spleen, paraspinal muscle, subcutaneous fat
